newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian democracy faces test in local polls.
newsitem.headline: Albanian democracy faces test in local polls.

text.p: Albania votes on Sunday in local elections seen by the West as a fresh test of its commitment to democracy, five months after a disputed general election.

President Sali Berisha's Democratic Party and the opposition Socialists both worked hard to persuade the 2.2 million voters that their policies offered the best prospects for Albania's towns and communes.
"I invite all Albanian voters to choose the Democratic Party candidates, the blue locomotive that will take Tirana into Europe," Berisha told the Democrats' final rally.
"Tomorrow it will be a fight to the end," ran the headline in Albania's biggest daily, Koha Jone.

The Socialists, reformed heirs to the communists, said they were confident of winning in a fair vote but they accused the Democrats of manipulating the electoral register and denying Socialist officials proper access to voting preparations.

Similar accusations marred the general election in May and June. Most opposition parties withdrew from that vote alleging ballot-rigging and intimidation -- charges upheld by some international observers.

The United States and the European Union have sent a clear signal to Berisha's conservative government that they will watch the local polls closely for signs that Albania is conforming to democratic norms.

There have already been some tussles between Tirana and international observers. The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) withdrew its monitors after the Albanian government rejected one of its team lists.

The Council of Europe, which will coordinate monitoring by 500 observers, deplored the OSCE's absence, but delegation head Victor Ruffy, a Swiss socialist, said he was optimistic that the local elections would run smoothly.
"We are satisfied that the electoral commission has taken our recommendations seriously and that the good will of the Democratic Party is present," he told Reuters.
Polls open at 8:00 a.m. local time (0600 gmt) for the elections for councils at town, district and communal level and close at 9:00 p.m. (19:00 GMT).
Final results were not expected before the middle of the week, but the U.S. Republican Institute will hold an exit poll in cooperation with Albania's Pikpamja Shqiptare foundation.
The toughest fight is expected in Tirana where all parties put forward heavyweight candidates for the post of mayor, held by the Democrats for the past four years.
In the last local polls in July 1992, the Socialists won more town halls than the Democrats but the governing party took all the big cities, including Durres, Shkoder, Fier and Vlore.
The Democrats also won 43.5 percent of district councils to the Socialists' 41 percent, but the latter got slightly more support in the communal vote.
